units.title: The Reproductive System
units.intro: **Primary** characters = the gonads and genitalia you are born with. **Secondary** = puberty changes (voice, hair, breasts, hips) driven by sex hormones.

cards.title: 2.1 Primary and Secondary Sexual Characteristics
body: **Reproduction** is a biological process in which new individuals are produced from their parent(s).
Reproduction is important in ensuring the continuity of life and/or the species.
Reproduction also increases the number of individuals of a species.
In asexual reproduction only one parent produces offspring of the same genetic makeup.
Part or parts of an organism break off to produce more of the same kind, or the organism divides into two or more parts.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following is considered a primary male sexual characteristic?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define primary sexual characteristics**
Primary sexual characteristics refer to the anatomical structures directly involved in reproduction that are present at birth.
**Step 2: Identify from options**
Testes and the penis are reproductive organs present at birth.
Deep voice, broad shoulders, and facial hair are secondary sexual characteristics that emerge during puberty.

cards.answer: The presence of the testes and penis

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: The scrotum maintains the temperature of the testes at which of the following ranges relative to core body temperature?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand testicular temperature requirements**
Viable spermatogenesis requires a temperature slightly lower than the core body temperature of $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
**Step 2: Identify the scrotum function**
The scrotum is situated outside the pelvic cavity, cooling the testes by approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature.
**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which cells in the interstitial tissue of the testes produce the androgen testosterone?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify cell types in the testes**
Seminiferous tubules contain spermatogonia and Sertoli cells. The interstitial spaces between the tubules contain Leydig cells.

**Step 2: Match with hormone function**
Leydig cells produce androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Leydig cells**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the function of the acrosome located at the head of a mature sperm cell?

options.A: To pack mitochondria for metabolic energy
options.B: To contain hydrolytic enzymes to penetrate the egg membranes
options.C: To provide motility for the sperm cell
options.D: To store glycogen for long-term survival

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand sperm head anatomy**
The head of the sperm contains the nucleus and is capped by the acrosome.

**Step 2: Define acrosome function**
The acrosome contains digestive enzymes that dissolve the outer layers of the secondary oocyte during fertilization.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **To contain hydrolytic enzymes to penetrate the egg membranes**.

cards.title: Puberty and sexual characters
body: **Primary sexual characters** are the reproductive organs present at birth (testes or ovaries). **Secondary sexual characters** develop at puberty under hormones: in boys (testosterone): deeper voice, facial and body hair, broader shoulders, bigger muscles; in girls (oestrogen): breasts develop, hips widen, menstruation begins, body hair grows.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: Mucous - like fluid that lubricate the end of penis
options.B: Milky fluid that neutralizes the byproducts of the sperm

cards.why: The **seminal vesicles** produce about 60% of the volume of semen. This fluid is **alkaline** (to neutralize vaginal acidity) and contains fructose (energy for sperm) and **prostaglandins** (to stimulate contractions in the female reproductive tract).

cards.title: 2.2 The Male Reproductive System
body: The male reproductive system consists of the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, Cowper’s gland, prostate gland, scrotum, and penis.
Testes: Testes, also called testicles, are the primary sex organs (gonads) of the male reproductive system.
The two testes are positioned outside the body cavity, one at either side of the penis.
The testes are ovoid structures about five centimetres in length and three centimetres in diameter.
**Testes** are the site in which the sperm cells (spermatozoa) and male sex hormones are produced.

cards.title: Male path
body: Testis (sperm + testosterone) → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra. Glands (prostate, seminal vesicle) add fluid. Sperm like a slightly cooler bag — that is why testes hang outside.

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.q: The male reproductive system **does not** include
cards.why: The male reproductive system consists of the testes, scrotum, penis, and glands like the prostate and epididymis. The **vulva** is the collective term for the external female genitalia, thus it is not part of the male system.

cards.title: Female path
body: Ovary (egg + oestrogen/progesterone) → oviduct (fertilisation address) → uterus (implants) → cervix → vagina.

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: FSH grows a follicle; oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining; LH surge ~day 14 ovulates; corpus luteum makes progesterone to keep the lining; if no embryo, progesterone falls and the lining is shed (menstruation).

cards.title: Mnemonic — FOLP
body: FSH → Oestrogen → LH → Progesterone. “First Open the Lining, then Protect it.”

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: **Fertilisation** in the oviduct. Zygote → blastocyst implants. Placenta feeds and exchanges gases; amniotic sac cushions. Birth: oxytocin (posterior pituitary) helps contractions.
**Contraception** methods: barrier, hormonal (stop ovulation), IUD, natural / calendar (least reliable), sterilisation. Exam: name the method and the *how* (block sperm / stop egg / stop implant).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Menstruation
body: After ovulation, if the ovum is fertilized by a sperm cell, a zygote is formed.
The corpus luteum produces progesterone, a hormone which causes the thickening of the uterine wall, in preparation to receive the fertilized ovum.
The endometrial wall and the unfertilized ovum is discharged with blood from the vagina.
After menstruation, the uterine lining begins to build up again.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Hormonal Control of Reproduction
body: Reproductive processes are controlled by a variety of hormones.
The hormonal mechanisms that influence the reproductive system involve the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, testes and ovaries.
The hypothalamus of the brain produces a chemical substance, such as the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Gn-RH) that travels to the pituitary gland.
Before puberty a small amount of testosterone and other androgens are available in the male’s body.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Fertilization and Pregnancy
body: Ovulation occurs roughly every 28 days, where one ovum is released alternatively by each of the two ovaries.
By ciliary action of the cells lining the fallopian tube, the ovum travels down the tube, where it may become fertilized by a sperm cell.
The ovum lives for only about 24 hours after it is released from the ovary.
During sexual intercourse or copulation, three to five million sperm cells per cubic centimetre of semen are released.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Child birth
body: Towards the end of gestation, the thick wall of the uterus begins to undergo regular powerful contractions, or labour.
The abdominal wall contracts; eventually the amnion is broken and amniotic fluid flows out through the vagina.
The fetus, with its head lying towards the cervix, gradually emerges through the vagina.
The portion of the umbilical cord remaining in the mother and the placenta are forced out by contractions of the abdominal and uterine walls.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which male accessory sex gland secretes a thin, alkaline fluid containing proteolytic enzymes that liquefy semen?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify male accessory glands**
The glands are the seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.

**Step 2: Analyze prostate secretions**
The prostate gland secretes a slightly alkaline, milky fluid that contains enzymes to liquefy the semen clot after ejaculation.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Prostate gland**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the structural and functional relationship between the ovaries and the fallopian tubes?

options.A: The ovaries are physically fused to the fallopian tubes to prevent egg loss.
options.B: The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.
options.C: Ovaries develop inside the fallopian tubes during fetal life.
options.D: The fallopian tubes secrete estrogen to stimulate ovarian follicle development.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze female reproductive anatomy**
The ovaries and fallopian tubes are not physically continuous. The opening of the fallopian tube lies close to the ovary.

**Step 2: Understand egg capture**
The funnel-shaped end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections (fimbriae) that capture the released oocyte and draw it into the tube.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.**

cards.title: 2.4 Contraception
body: Contraception can be defined as any means used to prevent a pregnancy.
Birth control includes the use of devices, drugs or surgery.
A family may be forced to determine the number of children it would like to have for reasons such as finance, the mother’s health, etc.
Contraception is used to avoid unwanted pregnancies in young girls who are not ready to take care of children.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During oogenesis, the unequal division of cytoplasm results in the production of which of the following?

options.B: One diploid zygote and three polar bodies
options.C: One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body

cards.why:
**Step 1: Examine oogenesis division**
In meiosis I, the primary oocyte divides unequally.

**Step 2: Identify the products**
It yields one large haploid secondary oocyte (retaining most of the cytoplasm and nutrients) and one small, non-functional first polar body.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which hormone experiences a massive surge around day 14 of the menstrual cycle, directly triggering ovulation?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review hormonal feedback leading to ovulation**
Rising estrogen levels from growing follicles trigger positive feedback, causing a rapid release of anterior pituitary hormones.

**Step 2: Identify the specific ovulation trigger**
The surge in Luteinizing Hormone ($$LH$$) is the direct trigger that causes the dominant follicle to rupture and release the egg.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Luteinizing Hormone ($$LH$$)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections such as HIV?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Most methods only prevent pregnancy.

**Step 2:** A condom is a physical barrier that stops semen and body fluids passing between partners.

**Step 3:** So it reduces the risk of STIs as well as pregnancy.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

In asexual reproduction, only one parent is required to generate offspring and no gametes or sex cells are involved.
Alternately, in sexual reproduction two individuals of the opposite sex parents are involved.
The parents produce gametes or sex cells.
The primary sexual characters are the genital organs, while secondary sexual characteristics are those anatomical and behavioural changes that take place during puberty or adolescence.

questions.q: A health educator at the hospital in Keren traces the route followed by sperm from the site of their formation to the point where they leave the male body through the urethra. According to the unit's SEVEN UP pathway, how many structures does a spermatozoon pass through during this journey, and what are they in order?

options.A: 4 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, urethra
options.B: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, penis
options.C: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, penis
options.D: 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

questions.answer: D
why: **Recall the SEVEN UP acronym.** The memory aid SEVEN UP gives the path of sperm: S = Seminiferous tubules, E = Epididymis, V = Vas deferens, E = Ejaculatory duct, N = Nothing (a placeholder, not a structure), U = Urethra, P = Penis. Only the six lettered structures carry sperm; the N entry is a memory aid with no anatomical counterpart.

**Check each structure against its stated role.** Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis; the epididymis stores spermatozoa and allows them to acquire motility; the vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum and loops over the urinary bladder; the ejaculatory duct is where the vas deferens joins; the urethra is the final tube; and the penis delivers semen.

**Reject the distractor pathways.** Options A and B place the vas deferens before the epididymis, but sperm enter the epididymis directly from the tubules and only later are propelled into the vas deferens. Options B and C omit the ejaculatory duct, which the unit explicitly lists between the vas deferens and the urethra. Options A and C also stop at the urethra and drop the penis.
**Count and conclude.** Six lettered structures remain once the placeholder N is excluded, giving the order seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: During a laboratory lesson in Asmara, a student models the pathway of seminal fluid by dropping coloured water at each named structure in turn. If she starts at the epididymis and ends at the ejaculatory duct, how many structures has she labelled along this stretch, and what are they in order?
questions.answer: 3 structures: epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct
why: **Locate the starting structure.** The SEVEN UP sequence places the epididymis immediately after the seminiferous tubules; within the epididymis sperm reside for several weeks and undergo biochemical maturation to acquire motility and fertilizing capability.

**Move to the next structure.** During sexual arousal, mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens, the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum, traverses the inguinal canal into the abdominal cavity, and loops over the urinary bladder.
**Identify the end point.** The vas deferens loops over the urinary bladder to join the ejaculatory duct, which is the stated end of this stretch.
**Count and conclude.** Labelling the epididymis, the vas deferens and the ejaculatory duct gives three structures in that order.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A student in Massawa repeatedly writes the male pathway as seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis. How many structures are in the wrong order, and what is the correct arrangement of those structures?

why: **Compare with SEVEN UP.** The correct SEVEN UP order is seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis. questions.q: A clinical technician in Asmara records a man's core body temperature as $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The unit states that spermatogenesis cannot occur effectively at core body temperature, and that the scrotum maintains an optimal microenvironment approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core body temperature. Calculate the full optimal scrotal temperature range, then state which of the following scrotal measurements would fall inside that range: $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ or $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
questions.answer: Optimal scrotal range = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$; the only measurement inside this range is $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
why: **State the governing principle.** The scrotum holds the testes outside the pelvic cavity so that sperm production occurs several degrees below core temperature, because high temperatures degrade the key germinal enzymes needed for spermatogenesis. The permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.
**Compute the upper end of the range.** The upper end is only $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compute the lower end of the range.** The lower end is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The optimal range is therefore $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ inclusive.

**Test each candidate measurement.** Compare each value with the interval $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C} \leq T \leq 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. For $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference from core is $$4.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which lies between $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ and $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it is inside. For $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference is only $$2.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; for $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$1.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; and for $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$0.8^{\circ}\text{C}$$. All three are less than $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature and therefore lie above $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, outside the range.
**Conclude.** The optimal scrotal temperature range is $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and of the four measurements only $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ falls within it.

questions.q: At a clinic in Massawa the ambient heat is high, and a technician notes that a man's testes are held at the extreme cool end of the permitted range while his core temperature reads $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. If the permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, calculate the temperature of the testes and state how many degrees cooler than core temperature this is.
questions.answer: Testicular temperature = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature
why: **Identify the relevant end of the range.** The extreme cool end corresponds to the largest permitted differential, which the unit gives as $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature. Under warm conditions the dartos and cremaster muscles relax to promote heat loss, which drives the testes toward this cool end.

**Substitute the core temperature.** Using core body temperature $$= 37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, the extreme cool testicular temperature is $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Check against the full range.** The full range spans $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is indeed the lowest value in that interval.

**State the cooling differential.** Subtracting the testicular temperature from the core temperature gives $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 32.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so the testes are held $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

questions.q: A man in Asmara takes a prolonged hot bath and his scrotal temperature rises to $$36.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ while his core temperature remains $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. Calculate how far this scrotal temperature lies below core temperature, and state whether it satisfies the $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential required for effective spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, so it does not satisfy the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential and spermatogenesis is impaired
why: **Calculate the actual differential.** The differential is core temperature minus scrotal temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 36.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compare with the required differential.** Effective spermatogenesis requires the testes to be approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core temperature. The measured differential of $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is smaller than the minimum of $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it falls short of the requirement.

**Relate the shortfall to enzyme function.** Spermatogenesis cannot proceed effectively at temperatures close to core body temperature because heat degrades key germinal enzymes. A differential of only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ leaves the testes far too warm for normal germ-cell development.

**Conclude.** The hot bath leaves the testes only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, which fails the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential, so sperm production is impaired.

questions.q: At a reproductive health session in Keren, a facilitator explains that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of the total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$, with the remainder coming from the bulbourethral glands and the spermatozoa themselves. If a single ejaculation has a total volume of $$3.0\text{ mL}$$, calculate the volume contributed by the seminal vesicles, the volume contributed by the prostate gland, and the combined volume contributed by all remaining sources.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.8\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.9\text{ mL}$$; all remaining sources $$= 0.3\text{ mL}$$ (together these sum to the $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ total).
why: **Identify the known quantities.** Total semen volume $$= 3.0\text{ mL}$$. Seminal vesicle contribution $$= 60\%$$ of total. Prostate gland contribution $$= 30\%$$ of total. The bulbourethral glands and spermatozoa account for whatever remains.

**Calculate the seminal vesicle volume.** Multiply the total volume by the seminal vesicle fraction: $$0.60 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 1.8\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid supplies fructose as metabolic fuel for sperm and prostaglandins that trigger contractions in the female reproductive tract, which is consistent with this gland providing the bulk of semen volume.

**Calculate the prostate gland volume.** Multiply the total volume by the prostate fraction: $$0.30 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.9\text{ mL}$$. This thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid contains citric acid and proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

**Calculate the remaining volume.** First find the remaining percentage: $$100\% - 60\% - 30\% = 10\%$$. Then apply it: $$0.10 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.3\text{ mL}$$. This residue corresponds to the clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands together with the spermatozoa.
**Check the total.** Add the parts: $$1.8\text{ mL} + 0.9\text{ mL} + 0.3\text{ mL} = 3.0\text{ mL}$$, which matches the stated total volume, so the calculation is consistent.

questions.q: A laboratory in Asmara receives a semen sample of $$2.5\text{ mL}$$ for analysis. Using the unit's values of $$60\%$$ for the seminal vesicles, $$30\%$$ for the prostate gland and the remaining percentage for the bulbourethral glands plus spermatozoa, calculate the volume contributed by each of the three components.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.5\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.75\text{ mL}$$; bulbourethral glands plus spermatozoa $$= 0.25\text{ mL}$$
why: **Set out the sample volume and fractions.** Total volume $$= 2.5\text{ mL}$$, seminal vesicle fraction $$= 0.60$$, prostate fraction $$= 0.30$$, and the remaining fraction is $$1 - 0.60 - 0.30 = 0.10$$.
**Compute the seminal vesicle share.** $$0.60 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 1.5\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fructose- and prostaglandin-rich fluid is the largest single contributor to semen volume.

**Compute the prostate share.** $$0.30 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.75\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid with proteolytic enzymes neutralizes vaginal acidity and liquefies the semen coagulum after ejaculation.
**Compute the remaining share.** $$0.10 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.25\text{ mL}$$, representing the clear lubricating mucus of the bulbourethral glands plus the spermatozoa.
**Verify the total.** $$1.5\text{ mL} + 0.75\text{ mL} + 0.25\text{ mL} = 2.5\text{ mL}$$, matching the sample volume.

questions.q: During a health talk in Barentu, a facilitator states that in one ejaculation the seminal vesicles contributed $$1.2\text{ mL}$$. Given that the seminal vesicles supply approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume, calculate the total volume of that ejaculate and the volume contributed by the prostate gland.
questions.answer: Total ejaculate volume $$= 2.0\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland contribution $$= 0.6\text{ mL}$$
why: **Set up the percentage relation.** The seminal vesicle volume equals $$60\%$$ of the total, so total volume $$= \dfrac{\text{seminal vesicle volume}}{0.60}$$.
**Compute the total volume.** Substitute the known part: total $$= \dfrac{1.2\text{ mL}}{0.60} = 2.0\text{ mL}$$.
**Compute the prostate volume.** The prostate contributes $$30\%$$ of the same total: $$0.30 \times 2.0\text{ mL} = 0.6\text{ mL}$$.

**Check the remaining component.** The remaining $$10\%$$ is $$0.10 \times 2.0\text{ mL} = 0.2\text{ mL}$$, and $$1.2\text{ mL} + 0.6\text{ mL} + 0.2\text{ mL} = 2.0\text{ mL}$$, confirming the total.

questions.q: A man in Massawa has been unable to conceive with his partner for two years. Semen analysis shows that sperm are being produced in normal numbers but almost all of them are immotile and none has acquired fertilizing capability, while the man's reproductive hormone levels are normal. Using only the structures and functions described in this unit, identify the single structure whose function is most likely impaired, and justify your answer with two functions of that structure.
questions.answer: The epididymis. It normally stores spermatozoa and provides the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability; normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm point to failure of exactly these two functions.
why: **Note that sperm production itself is intact.** The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis and the Sertoli cells provide nutrients and structural support to developing germ cells. Because sperm are produced in normal numbers, this function is clearly not the problem. The acrosome, which carries the hydrolytic enzymes needed to digest the egg's protective layers, is also formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, so the production line is working.

**Identify which function is missing.** The two missing features are motility and fertilizing capability. The unit states that sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability during their residence in the epididymis, where they undergo biochemical maturation over several weeks.

**Match the missing functions to the correct structure.** The epididymis is the crescent-shaped tubule coiled on the superior-posterior margin of each testis in which spermatozoa reside for several weeks. Its two functions are (i) storing spermatozoa and (ii) facilitating the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability. An impairment of this structure explains normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm.

**Confirm that the other ducts are not implicated.** The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular duct that simply transports mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct; it does not mature sperm. The unit also notes that mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens only during sexual arousal, whereas the immotility described here is a property of the sperm themselves, present regardless of arousal.

**Conclude.** The impaired structure is the epididymis, because the sperm have normal production but lack precisely the two properties, motility and fertilizing capability, that the epididymis confers during maturation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man in Asmara undergoes a vasectomy in which the vas deferens is cut and sealed. His testes continue to produce sperm and his Leydig cells continue to secrete testosterone. Explain, using only the unit's description of the male tract and of semen composition, what happens to the sperm produced after the operation and why the operation does not reduce his testosterone levels.
questions.answer: Sperm are still produced in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis, but they can no longer pass beyond the sealed vas deferens, so they are not included in the ejaculate; testosterone is unaffected because it is secreted by the Leydig cells, which the unit places under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary, not under the control of the vas deferens.
why: **Locate the cut in the pathway.** The vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that carries mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis out of the scrotum, through the inguinal canal and over the urinary bladder to the ejaculatory duct. Sealing it blocks this single transport route.

**Trace the fate of the sperm.** Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is unaffected, and sperm still pass into the epididymis to mature. However, they cannot be propelled beyond the blocked vas deferens, so no sperm reach the ejaculatory duct and urethra and none appear in the ejaculate, which is why vasectomy is a permanent surgical contraceptive method.

**Locate the source of testosterone.** In the interstitial space between adjacent seminiferous tubules lie the Leydig cells, which synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone from the anterior pituitary. These cells are entirely separate from the vas deferens.

**Explain why testosterone is unchanged.** Because the Leydig cells and the HPG axis that regulates them are untouched by the operation, testosterone secretion continues normally. Only the sperm delivery route, not the endocrine function of the testis, has been interrupted.

**Conclude.** After vasectomy, sperm are produced and matured but can no longer leave the tract, while testosterone levels remain normal because Leydig cells under LH control continue to secrete androgen independently of the vas deferens.

questions.q: A student in Keren claims that because the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release a clear fluid before ejaculation, that fluid must be the main carrier of sperm. Explain, using the unit's description of the male accessory glands, why this claim is incorrect, and state the two functions the bulbourethral glands actually perform.
questions.answer: The claim is incorrect because the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small clear, viscous pre-ejaculatory mucus; the bulk of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles (about 60%) and the prostate gland (about 30%). Their two functions are lubricating the urethra and neutralizing residual acidic urine prior to ejaculation.
why: **Establish the actual volume contributions.** The unit states that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$. Together these two glands account for about $$90\%$$ of semen, leaving only roughly $$10\%$$ for the bulbourethral gland secretion and the spermatozoa themselves.

**Show why the student's claim fails.** A secretion that forms only a small fraction of the ejaculate cannot be its main carrier of sperm. The spermatozoa themselves are the cellular component, suspended in the fluid vehicle formed mainly by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

**State the real functions of the bulbourethral glands.** The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus whose functions are to lubricate the urethra and to neutralize residual acidic urine before semen passes. These are preparatory and protective roles, not a sperm-carrying role.

**Conclude.** The claim is incorrect: the bulbourethral secretion is a minor pre-ejaculatory lubricating and neutralizing fluid, while the seminal vesicles and prostate gland provide the bulk of the semen volume.

questions.q: A man's blood testosterone level rises well above its normal stable value. Applying the negative feedback loop described in this unit, which of the following correctly states the resulting changes?

options.A: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to increase GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so testosterone production rises further.
options.B: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.
options.C: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion but on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so the two effects cancel and testosterone production is unchanged.
options.D: Testosterone acts directly on the seminiferous tubules to decrease spermatogenesis, and the reduced sperm numbers feed back on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release.

questions.answer: B
why: **Identify the axis being regulated.** Testosterone secretion is governed by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), which drives the anterior pituitary to release LH, and LH stimulates the Leydig cells of the testis to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

**State the direction of a negative feedback loop.** In negative feedback, a rise in the level of the final hormone in the chain suppresses the earlier steps of the chain. The unit states explicitly that as blood testosterone levels rise, testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, stabilizing hormone levels.

**Evaluate each option.** Option A describes positive feedback, in which rising testosterone would further increase GnRH and LH, which contradicts the stabilizing negative feedback the unit describes; it also misstates the effect on both organs. Option C is internally inconsistent, since the unit gives decreases at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. Option D introduces a sperm-count feedback signal that the unit never describes, and the unit's loop is defined by blood testosterone acting on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, not on the seminiferous tubules.

**Confirm the correct option and its consequence.** Option B matches the unit exactly: decreased GnRH and decreased LH. With less LH reaching the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells are less stimulated, testosterone secretion falls, and the elevated blood level is brought back down toward its stable value.
**Conclude.** Rising blood testosterone suppresses the HPG axis at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so option B is the correct statement of the feedback response.

questions.q: A laboratory report for a patient in Asmara shows a very low blood testosterone level together with an abnormally high LH level, and the hypothalamic GnRH secretion is found to be high. Which single structure does this pattern indicate is failing, and what is the normal response of that structure to LH?
questions.answer: The Leydig cells (interstitial cells) of the testis are failing. Normally LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, so unrepaired Leydig cells should raise testosterone output when LH is high.
why: **Read the pattern of hormones.** GnRH is high and LH is high, so the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary are both sending strong stimulatory signals down the HPG axis. The defect therefore lies below the pituitary.

**Identify the target of LH.** The unit states that the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells lying between adjacent seminiferous tubules, synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone secreted from the anterior pituitary.

**Explain why high LH with low testosterone is diagnostic.** If the Leydig cells were responding normally, a high LH level would drive testosterone production upward. Instead testosterone remains very low, so the Leydig cells are not responding to LH stimulation and are the failing structure.

**Account for the high upstream hormones.** Because testosterone is the signal that suppresses the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, low testosterone removes that inhibition. GnRH and LH therefore remain high, which is exactly what the report shows.
**Conclude.** The failing structure is the Leydig cell population of the testis, whose normal response to LH is to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

questions.q: A man in Keren receives a treatment that keeps his blood testosterone concentration artificially high for several weeks. Predict the effect of this treatment on the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone and Luteinizing Hormone, and explain how the treatment will affect the activity of his Leydig cells.
questions.answer: GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus and LH release from the anterior pituitary will both decrease through negative feedback; with less LH stimulation the Leydig cells will become less active and their own testosterone secretion will fall.
why: **Recognise the feedback signal.** Blood testosterone is the final hormone of the HPG axis and acts as the inhibitory signal on the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. An artificially raised level therefore acts as a strong inhibitory signal.
**Predict the hypothalamic response.** The hypothalamus responds by decreasing its secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone, the hormone that normally drives the anterior pituitary.
**Predict the pituitary response.** The anterior pituitary responds to the raised testosterone directly, as well as to the reduced GnRH, by decreasing its release of Luteinizing Hormone.

**Trace the effect on Leydig cells.** Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testosterone when stimulated by LH. With LH release suppressed, the Leydig cells receive less stimulation and become less active, so the testis's own contribution to blood testosterone declines even while the external treatment maintains a high total level.
**Conclude.** Sustained high blood testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH through negative feedback, and the reduced LH stimulation in turn lowers the secretory activity of the Leydig cells.
